note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Acute-onset shortness of breath and chest tightness beginning 2–3 days ago, first noted while running with a friend (exertional trigger).
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Symptoms began 2–3 days ago during running; now occurs with brisk walking and on exertion; described as worsening over the last 2–3 days.
- ENT-relevant symptoms:
  - Throat swelling/closure sensation: none reported.
  - Voice change/hoarseness: none reported.
  - Dysphagia/odynophagia: none reported.
  - Drooling: none reported.
  - Nasal/ocular symptoms: baseline hay fever reported; no acute nasal/ocular complaints documented.
  - Stridor/noisy breathing: wheeze reported (patient states “wheezing a bit”).
  - Dyspnea: yes — shortness of breath with exertion and at times at rest.
  - Distribution of swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): none reported.
  - Ear/neck symptoms: none reported.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - Prior asthma exacerbation approximately 3–4 years ago.
  - No prior hospital admissions for asthma.
  - No recollection of prior oral steroid courses.
  - Last asthma review with nurse about 2 years ago.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: hay fever (patient stated “I have hay fever”); no drug allergies reported.
  - Current inhalers/medications (as stated):
    - Salbutamol (blue inhaler) — rescue use; dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - “Brown” inhaler (Clenil) — preventer; patient stated prior use at three puffs twice daily (doctor advised increase to four puffs twice daily).
    - Cetraben topical — mentioned by patient; dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Hydrocortisone topical — mentioned by patient; dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Conflict noted: patient initially said “Flanel Bactroban” then corrected to “Cetraben and Hydrocortisone.”
- Any relevant social context:
  - Symptoms started while running with a friend. No other persons reported present during this consultation.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: none stated.
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - Wheeze and cough reported by patient.
  - Shortness of breath on exertion and at times at rest.
  - No stridor recorded.
- Mental status and associated features:
  - No dizziness or syncope reported.
- Vitals and examination findings:
  - Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient during consult:
  - Not recorded.

Assessment:
- Clinical impression:
  - Suspected acute asthma exacerbation (exertion-triggered), previously controlled, now worsening over 2–3 days with wheeze, cough and exertional dyspnea.
- Key justifications:
  - Symptoms began during running and have progressed over several days; increased use of salbutamol rescue inhaler; prior asthma history with last exacerbation 3–4 years ago; use of preventer inhaler (Clenil) but possible under-dosing until advised to increase.
- Additional notes:
  - No features suggestive of anaphylaxis or upper airway swelling in the transcript.
  - Conflict noted regarding topical medications named (Flanel Bactroban vs Cetraben) and whether patient has eczema.

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Increase brown inhaler (Clenil) to four puffs twice daily (advice to implement while awaiting GP review).
  - Continue/use salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed, up to every 2–4 hours as interim measure.
  - Arrange face-to-face GP review within the next few days for chest examination, peak flow measurement and further management.
  - Possible treatments after assessment: antibiotics and/or oral steroids depending on clinical findings and peak flow.
- Specific instructions provided to patient (exact phrasing from transcript):
  - “You can use your blue inhaler as and when. You can use it maximum about every two to four, four hours, but if you're using it that often that means pretty much that, you know, your asthma is really bad.”
  - “If your breathing is getting really worse, then you would need to take yourself to A and E. You shouldn't wait for our appointment.”
  - “If you breathing's getting worse and you've not seen us, do take your puffs to A and E.”
- Escalation criteria / red flags advised:
  - Worsening breathlessness, increasing frequency of rescue inhaler use (approaching every 2–4 hours), inability to speak in full sentences, signs of airway compromise — go to A&E immediately.
- Follow-up:
  - Face-to-face GP appointment recommended within a few days for chest exam and peak flow; management may include oral steroids and/or antibiotics based on findings.
  - No referral to ENT or allergy documented in the transcript.
- Emergency contact instructions (exact as stated in transcript):
  - “If your breathing is getting really worse, then you would need to take yourself to A and E. You shouldn't wait for our appointment.”
  - “If you breathing's getting worse and you've not seen us, do take your puffs to A and E.”

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Current vital signs (RR, HR, SpO2, temperature) — not recorded.
  - Objective peak flow reading during this exacerbation — not recorded (patient quoted baseline ~380 L/min).
  - Current exact doses, routes and frequencies for inhalers and topical medications (some dosing not documented).
  - Use of spacer with inhaler — not documented.
  - Smoking status, occupational exposures, and recent upper respiratory infection symptoms — not documented.
  - Asthma action plan and availability of oral steroid supply at home — not documented.
  - No documentation regarding consideration of oral steroids given current exacerbation (doctor discussed possibility pending assessment).
  - No information about auto-injector or prior anaphylaxis (not applicable per transcript).
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Patient medication list unclear: said “Flanel Bactroban” initially, then corrected to “Cetraben and Hydrocortisone.” Conflict noted.
  - Unclear whether patient has a diagnosis of eczema (patient first implied topical meds, then said family history of eczema).
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally understandable. Some sections unclear or disfluent regarding topical medication names and prior eczema history. No significant background noise reported.
